item.title: Salesforce Web-to-Lead & Web-to-Case Cheat Sheet: Forms, Limits, reCAPTCHA and Admin Interview Q&A (Day 24/30)
item.description: Turn website visitors into records without lifting a finger. Web-to-Lead and Web-to-Case come up in almost every admin interview. A generated HTML form…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
Turn website visitors into records without lifting a finger. Web-to-Lead and Web-to-Case come up in almost every admin interview.

The 4 Building Blocks

Block What it is Key point
Web-to-Lead HTML form makes leads 500 per day
Web-to-Case HTML form makes cases 5,000 per day
Form Fields Standard plus custom Use the field ID
Protection reCAPTCHA and routing Stop the spam

Interview Q&A

1. What is Web-to-Lead?

A generated HTML form that creates leads from your website.

Tip: No hand coding needed.

2. What are the daily limits?

Web-to-Lead allows 500 a day. Web-to-Case allows 5,000 a day.

Tip: Plan for busy days.

3. How do you add custom fields?

Add the field to the HTML using its field ID.

Tip: Test after adding.

4. What stops spam?

Turn on reCAPTCHA and validate the fields.

Tip: Bots love open forms.

5. How do leads get an owner?

Lead assignment rules route them, or the default owner takes them.

Tip: Rules run automatically.

6. Can customers get a reply?

Yes, auto-response rules email them on creation.

Tip: Keep the template clear.

Scenario Question

"Website enquiries must become leads for sales. How?"

  1. Generate the form in Setup
  2. Add reCAPTCHA and a return URL
  3. Set assignment and auto-response
  4. Test with a sample submit

Quick Cheat Sheet

  • Form = generated HTML
  • Lead cap = 500 a day
  • Case cap = 5,000 a day
  • Spam = reCAPTCHA
  • Owner = assignment rule
  • Reply = auto-response

Key Takeaways

  • Generate the form, do not hand build
  • Protect it with reCAPTCHA
  • Route and reply automatically
  • Test before going live

Which form is on your site? Tell me in the comments!

item.title: Day 1/120 – #120DaysOfAWS: IAM, the Front Door to Everything in AWS
item.description: Every AWS action, from launching an EC2 instance to reading an S3 object, goes through one question: is this identity allowed to do this? IAM (Identity and…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
Every AWS action, from launching an EC2 instance to reading an S3 object, goes through one question: is this identity allowed to do this? IAM (Identity and Access Management) answers it, so I'm starting here.

The 5 building blocks

  • Users: a person or app with long-term credentials.
  • Groups: a collection of users that share permissions. Attach policies to groups, not to individual people.
  • Roles: temporary credentials that anyone or anything can assume. This is how EC2, Lambda and cross-account access should work.
  • Policies: JSON documents that say who can do what on which resource.
  • MFA: a second factor that protects the account if a password leaks.

How a policy reads

{
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Action": "s3:GetObject",
  "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket/*"
}

Effect, Action and Resource are the three parts to check first. An explicit Deny always beats an Allow, and anything not allowed is denied by default.

What I did hands-on today

  • Checked my IAM dashboard: MFA is on for my root user and my IAM user, and I have no stale access keys.
  • Created a user group called ReadOnlyTeam and attached the AWS-managed ReadOnlyAccess policy.
  • Used the Policy Simulator to test two S3 actions against that group:
    • s3:GetObject was Allowed (explicit allow).
    • s3:DeleteObject was Denied (implicit deny: no policy allows it, so it's blocked by default).
  • Ran the same test against my own user, which has AdministratorAccess, and both actions were Allowed. The same action gets a different answer depending on which policies are attached, which is why least privilege matters.

3 habits I'm keeping

  1. Never use the root user for daily work.
  2. Grant least privilege: start with nothing and add only what's needed.
  3. Prefer roles over long-lived access keys.

Tomorrow (Day 2): writing a custom IAM policy from scratch.

item.title: Salesforce Queues & Assignment Rules Cheat Sheet: Routing Leads and Cases and Admin Interview Q&A (Day 23/30)
item.description: Every lead and case needs an owner. Queues hold them, rules route them. Queues and assignment rules come up in almost every admin interview. A shared owner…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
Every lead and case needs an owner. Queues hold them, rules route them. Queues and assignment rules come up in almost every admin interview.

The 4 Building Blocks

Block What it is Key point
Queues Shared record owner Members claim records
Assignment Rules Leads and cases only Entries run in order
Rule Entries Criteria then assignee First match wins
Activation One active per object Tick the box to apply

Interview Q&A

1. What is a queue?

A shared owner that holds records until a member claims them.

Tip: Records wait in it.

2. Who can be queue members?

Users, roles, public groups and more.

Tip: Add groups, not people.

3. Which objects get rules?

Assignment rules work for leads and cases only.

Tip: Not custom objects.

4. How do rule entries work?

Entries run in order and the first match assigns the record.

Tip: Order matters.

5. How many rules can be active?

One active assignment rule per object at a time.

Tip: Activate one at a time.

6. Why did a record skip the rule?

The assign using active rules box was not ticked.

Tip: Tick it when saving.

Scenario Question

"New web leads must route to regional teams. How?"

  1. Create a queue per region
  2. Add rule entries by country
  3. Activate the lead rule
  4. Test with a sample lead

Quick Cheat Sheet

  • Queue = shared owner
  • Rule = leads, cases
  • Entry = criteria + owner
  • Order = first match
  • Active = one rule
  • Checkbox = apply rule

Key Takeaways

  • Queues stop records going unowned
  • Order entries specific to general
  • Add a catch all entry
  • Test before you activate

Queue or direct owner? Tell me in the comments!

item.title: Salesforce Custom Metadata vs Custom Settings Cheat Sheet: Deploy, Hierarchy and Admin Interview Q&A (Day 22/30)
item.description: Never hardcode a value. Pick the home that fits how it must travel. Custom metadata versus custom settings comes up in almost every admin interview. App…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
Never hardcode a value. Pick the home that fits how it must travel. Custom metadata versus custom settings comes up in almost every admin interview.

The 4 Building Blocks

Block What it is Key point
Custom Settings List or hierarchy type Data stays in the org
Custom Metadata Config stored as records Deploys with metadata
Hierarchy Values per user or profile Settings only
Use Cases Rates, flags, mappings Not for big data

Interview Q&A

1. What are custom settings?

App config kept in a cached table, as a List or Hierarchy type.

Tip: Fast to read in code.

2. What is custom metadata?

Custom types whose records are metadata, so they deploy between orgs.

Tip: Records travel with deploys.

3. Biggest difference?

Custom metadata records deploy. Custom settings data does not.

Tip: The interview favorite.

4. What is a hierarchy setting?

A setting with values per user, profile or org default.

Tip: Only in custom settings.

5. Can admins use them without code?

Yes, in formulas, validation rules and flows.

Tip: Skip hardcoding.

6. Which should you pick?

Metadata for deployable config. Settings for per user values.

Tip: Default to metadata.

Scenario Question

"A tax rate differs by region and must reach prod. How?"

  1. Create a custom metadata type
  2. Add one record per region
  3. Use it in a formula or flow
  4. Deploy with a change set

Quick Cheat Sheet

  • Settings = data stays
  • Metadata = deploys
  • Hierarchy = per user
  • Cache = fast reads
  • Hardcode = avoid
  • Default = metadata

Key Takeaways

  • Never hardcode values
  • Choose metadata when you deploy
  • Choose hierarchy for per user rules
  • Admins edit it without code

What do you still hardcode? Tell me in the comments!

item.title: Salesforce Data Backup & Recovery Cheat Sheet: Data Export, Recycle Bin and Admin Interview Q&A (Day 21/30)
item.description: Back up before you need it. Deleted data is only safe while a copy exists. Backup and recovery questions come up in almost every admin interview. A Setup…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
Back up before you need it. Deleted data is only safe while a copy exists. Backup and recovery questions come up in almost every admin interview.

The 4 Building Blocks

Block What it is Key point
Data Export Zip of CSV files Weekly or monthly
Recycle Bin Deleted records kept 15 days to restore
Metadata Setup is not in export Use sandboxes or Git
Recovery Restore from your files Plan before you need it

Interview Q&A

1. What is Data Export?

A Setup tool that creates a zip of CSV files of your data, weekly or monthly.

Tip: It exports records only.

2. How long are export files kept?

The download link expires after 48 hours, so download it quickly.

Tip: Save a copy elsewhere.

3. What is the Recycle Bin?

It holds deleted records for 15 days so you can restore them.

Tip: Hard delete skips it.

4. Is metadata in the export?

No. Data Export saves records, not setup. Use sandboxes, change sets or Git.

Tip: Back up data and setup.

5. Can Salesforce restore lost data?

The old recovery service was retired, so keep your own backups.

Tip: Do not rely on support.

6. What other backup options exist?

Data Loader, reports, the paid Backup and Restore, or AppExchange tools.

Tip: Pick by size and speed.

Scenario Question

"A user deleted 500 accounts by mistake. What now?"

  1. Check the Recycle Bin first
  2. Restore the deleted records
  3. Use the last export if they were purged
  4. Schedule regular exports

Quick Cheat Sheet

  • Export = records zip
  • Recycle Bin = 15 days
  • Link = 48 hours
  • Metadata = separate
  • Hard delete = gone
  • Schedule = weekly

Key Takeaways

  • Schedule exports, do not wait
  • Test your restore plan
  • Back up data and metadata
  • Limit who can delete

When did you last test a restore? Tell me in the comments!

item.title: Salesforce Roles & Role Hierarchy Cheat Sheet: Record Access, Profiles and Admin Interview Q&A (Day 20/30)
item.description: Access flows up the org chart. Roles open doors for managers, they never close them. Roles and the role hierarchy come up in almost every admin interview…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
Access flows up the org chart. Roles open doors for managers, they never close them. Roles and the role hierarchy come up in almost every admin interview.

The 4 Building Blocks

Block What it is Key point
Hierarchy Top down visibility Managers see below
Roles Jobs in the org chart One per user
Grant Access Using Hierarchies setting On for standard objects
Vs Profiles Roles = records Profiles = permissions

Interview Q&A

1. What is a role hierarchy?

A structure that gives managers access to records owned by people below them.

Tip: Access flows up, never down.

2. Role vs profile?

Roles control record access. Profiles control object and field permissions.

Tip: Data versus permissions.

3. Does a role restrict access?

No. It only opens access above a Private default, it never reduces it.

Tip: OWD sets the floor.

4. What is Grant Access Using Hierarchies?

A per object setting that lets higher roles see lower roles' records.

Tip: Always on for standard objects.

5. Can a user have many roles?

No. One role per user, but one role can hold many users.

Tip: One role each.

6. What if you delete a role?

You must reassign its users and child roles to another role first.

Tip: Plan before deleting.

Scenario Question

"A manager cannot see her team's accounts. Why?"

  1. Check the default access is Private
  2. Place her role above the team
  3. Confirm hierarchy access is on
  4. Verify who owns the records

Quick Cheat Sheet

  • Role = record access
  • Hierarchy = flows up
  • Profile = permissions
  • OWD = the floor
  • Branch = a region
  • One role = per user

Key Takeaways

  • Roles open access, never close it
  • Mirror the org chart, keep it simple
  • Cross branch? Use sharing rules
  • Few levels run faster

How deep is your role hierarchy? Tell me in the comments!

Following my 30-day daily blogging journey. Day 20 done, 10 to go.

item.title: Salesforce Lightning Record Pages Cheat Sheet: App Builder, Dynamic Forms and Admin Interview Q&A (Day 19/30)
item.description: Build the page each user needs with clicks, then show it to the right people. Lightning App Builder and record pages come up in almost every admin…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
Build the page each user needs with clicks, then show it to the right people. Lightning App Builder and record pages come up in almost every admin interview.

The 4 Building Blocks

Block What it is Key point
App Builder Drag and drop page tool Clicks, not code
Page Types App, home, record Pick the right one
Components Standard or custom blocks Drop onto the page
Activation Org, app or profile Assign to take effect

Interview Q&A

1. What is Lightning App Builder?

A drag and drop tool to build app, home and record pages without code.

Tip: Clicks before code.

2. What are the page types?

App pages, home pages and record pages, each for a different job.

Tip: Record pages show one record.

3. What are components?

Building blocks like the Highlights Panel and Related Lists you drop on a page.

Tip: Keep pages light and fast.

4. What are Dynamic Forms?

They show or hide fields by rules instead of one fixed layout.

Tip: They can replace extra layouts.

5. What is component visibility?

A filter that shows a component only when conditions are met, like profile or field value.

Tip: Less clutter for each user.

6. How do you activate a page?

Assign it as org default, app default, or by app, record type and profile.

Tip: The most specific one wins.

Scenario Question

"Reps need a cleaner Opportunity page. How?"

  1. Clone the standard record page
  2. Add components and set visibility
  3. Use Dynamic Forms for key fields
  4. Activate for the sales app

Quick Cheat Sheet

  • App Builder = page tool
  • Record page = one record
  • Dynamic Forms = field rules
  • Visibility = show if
  • Clone = safe start
  • Activation = who sees it

Key Takeaways

  • Clone, never edit the standard page
  • Hide what users do not need
  • Fewer components load faster
  • Test as the user profile

Which page would you clean up first? Tell me in the comments!

item.title: Salesforce Duplicate & Matching Rules Cheat Sheet: Block, Alert, Merge and Admin Interview Q&A (Day 18/30)
item.description: Stop messy duplicates before they land, and clean up the ones already in your data. Duplicate and matching rules are core data quality topics in any admin…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
Stop messy duplicates before they land, and clean up the ones already in your data. Duplicate and matching rules are core data quality topics in any admin interview.

The 4 Building Blocks

Block What it is Key point
Matching Rule Defines what is a match Compares chosen fields
Duplicate Rule Acts on a match Block or alert
Merge Combine up to 3 records Keeps one master
Report Lists found duplicates Review and clean

Interview Q&A

1. What is a matching rule?

It defines which fields to compare and how closely records must match.

Tip: Fuzzy or exact, field by field.

2. What is a duplicate rule?

It decides what happens on a match: block the save or allow it with an alert.

Tip: Matching finds, the rule acts.

3. Are there standard rules?

Salesforce ships standard rules for accounts, contacts and leads.

Tip: Activate them before customising.

4. Block or alert?

Block stops the save. Alert warns, then lets the user continue.

Tip: Start with alert, then tighten.

5. How do you merge?

Combine up to three records into one master, choosing which values to keep.

Tip: Check related records first.

6. What are the limits?

Rules check new saves, so existing duplicates need a separate clean up.

Tip: Clean first, then prevent.

Scenario Question

"Stop duplicate leads being created. How?"

  1. Activate the standard lead matching rule
  2. Create a duplicate rule on Lead
  3. Set the action to alert first
  4. Test, then merge old duplicates

Quick Cheat Sheet

  • Matching = finds matches
  • Duplicate rule = acts
  • Block = stops the save
  • Alert = warns the user
  • Merge = up to 3 records
  • Report = lists duplicates

Key Takeaways

  • Prevent and clean, do both
  • Start with alert, not block
  • Test with real data
  • Merge carefully, there is no undo

What is the messiest duplicate you have seen? Tell me in the comments!

Following my 30-day daily blogging journey. Day 18 done, 12 to go.

item.title: Salesforce Email Templates & Alerts Cheat Sheet: Merge Fields, Flow and Admin Interview Q&A (Day 17/30)
item.description: Write the email once, merge in the record data, and let automation send it at the right moment. Email templates and alerts are everyday admin work and a…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
Write the email once, merge in the record data, and let automation send it at the right moment. Email templates and alerts are everyday admin work and a common interview topic.

The 4 Building Blocks

Block What it is Key point
Template Reusable email layout Merge fields fill it in
Email Alert Sends a template Chosen recipients
Letterhead Logo and brand colours Wraps the template
Org-Wide Address Trusted From address Must be verified

Interview Q&A

1. What is an email template?

A reusable email with merge fields that fill in record data automatically.

Tip: Write once, reuse everywhere.

2. What template types exist?

Lightning templates use a builder. Classic ones are text, HTML and Visualforce.

Tip: Lightning is the modern default.

3. What is an email alert?

A saved action that sends a template to the recipients you choose.

Tip: The alert sends, Flow decides when.

4. How do you trigger one?

From a Flow or an approval process when your condition is met.

Tip: Use Flow for new work.

5. What are merge fields?

Placeholders like {!Contact.FirstName} swapped for real values when the email is sent.

Tip: Test with a real record.

6. What are the limits?

A daily send limit applies, and emails can bounce or land in spam.

Tip: Use an org-wide address.

Scenario Question

"Email the customer when a case is closed. How?"

  1. Create a template with merge fields

  2. Create an email alert using it

  3. Add it to a Flow on case closed

  4. Test with a real case

Quick Cheat Sheet

  • Template = reusable email

  • Alert = sends it

  • Merge field = record data

  • Letterhead = branding

  • Org-wide = trusted sender

  • Flow = decides when

Key Takeaways

  • Use merge fields, not typed names

  • Send from an org-wide address

  • Test before you activate

  • One template per purpose

Which email do you automate first? Tell me in the comments!

Following my 30-day daily blogging journey. Day 17 done, 13 to go.

item.title: Salesforce Sandboxes & Change Sets Cheat Sheet: Types, Validation and Admin Interview Q&A (Day 16/30)
item.description: Build safely away from live users, then move the changes to production the controlled way. Sandboxes and change sets are core admin deployment topics and a…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
Build safely away from live users, then move the changes to production the controlled way. Sandboxes and change sets are core admin deployment topics and a favourite interview question.

The 4 Building Blocks

Block What it is Key point
Sandbox Safe copy of production Build and test here
Outbound Set Built in the source org Uploaded to the target
Inbound Set Arrives in the target org Validate, then deploy
Validation Dry run with tests Saves nothing

Interview Q&A

1. What is a sandbox?

A copy of production metadata where you build and test changes safely, away from live users.

Tip: Never build in production.

2. What are the sandbox types?

Developer and Developer Pro copy metadata. Partial Copy adds sample data. Full copies everything.

Tip: Match the type to the test.

3. What is a change set?

A bundle of metadata components you send from one org to another connected org.

Tip: Metadata only, not data.

4. Outbound vs inbound?

Outbound is built and uploaded in the source org. Inbound waits in the target org to be validated and deployed.

Tip: Outbound out, inbound in.

5. Why validate first?

A validation runs the checks and tests without saving changes, so you know the deploy will pass.

Tip: Validate, then deploy.

6. What are the limits?

Change sets work only between connected orgs, some components are unsupported, and there is no version history or easy rollback.

Tip: Name the limits, then mention Git and CI/CD.

Scenario Question

"Move a new validation rule and layout to production. How?"

  1. Build and test it in a sandbox

  2. Add both to an outbound change set

  3. Upload to production and validate

  4. Deploy in a quiet window

Quick Cheat Sheet

  • Sandbox = safe copy of prod

  • Outbound = sent from source

  • Inbound = received in target

  • Validate = dry run

  • Apex = 75% test coverage

  • Limits = no rollback

Key Takeaways

  • Build in a sandbox only

  • Add every dependency to the set

  • Validate before you deploy

  • Deploy outside business hours

What was your first deployment? Tell me in the comments!

Following my 30-day daily blogging journey. Day 16 done, 14 to go.

item.title: Salesforce Data Import Wizard vs Data Loader Cheat Sheet: Upsert, Limits and Admin Interview Q&A (Day 15/30)
item.description: Two tools, one job. Pick by record volume, objects and whether you need to update or delete. This is one of the most common practical questions in a…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
Two tools, one job. Pick by record volume, objects and whether you need to update or delete. This is one of the most common practical questions in a Salesforce admin interview.

The 4 Building Blocks

Block What it is Key point
Import Wizard Browser tool for simple loads Up to 50,000 records
Data Loader Desktop app for big jobs Up to 5 million records
Upsert Update matches, insert the rest Matched by External ID
Export Back up data before a load Export or Export All

Interview Q&A

1. Wizard vs Data Loader?

The Wizard is simple and browser-based for up to 50,000 records. Data Loader handles far larger volumes and more objects.

Tip: Size and object decide.

2. What is an upsert?

It updates records that match and inserts the rest, matching on the record ID or an External ID field.

Tip: External IDs avoid duplicates.

3. What can Data Loader do?

Insert, update, upsert, delete, hard delete, export and export all, from the app or the command line.

Tip: Export All includes deleted rows.

4. How do you load related data?

Load parents first, then load children using IDs or External IDs to link them to their parents.

Tip: Parents before children.

5. What do you check after a load?

Open the success and error files, fix the failed rows, and reload only those.

Tip: Keep the error file.

6. How do you avoid a bad load?

Test in a sandbox, export a backup first, and check validation rules and automation that will fire.

Tip: Back up before you load.

Scenario Question

"Load 200,000 contacts from a CSV without duplicates. How do you do it?"

  1. Export a backup of existing contacts

  2. Clean the CSV and add an External ID

  3. Run Data Loader with upsert

  4. Check the success and error files

Quick Cheat Sheet

  • Wizard = up to 50,000 records

  • Loader = up to 5 million

  • Upsert = update or insert

  • External ID = match key

  • Parents = load first

  • Error file = fix and reload

Key Takeaways

  • Clean the data before loading

  • Test in a sandbox first

  • Export a backup beforehand

  • Keep success and error files

What was your biggest data load? Tell me in the comments!

Following my 30-day daily blogging journey. Day 15 done, 15 to go.

item.title: Salesforce Permission Sets & Groups Cheat Sheet: Profiles, Muting and Admin Interview Q&A (Day 14/30)
item.description: One profile, many permission sets. Start with minimum access, then add only what each person needs. It is the access-control answer interviewers expect…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
One profile, many permission sets. Start with minimum access, then add only what each person needs. It is the access-control answer interviewers expect from a modern admin.

The 4 Building Blocks

Block What it is Key point
Permission Set Adds access on top of a profile Grants only, never removes
Set Group Bundles sets for a job role Assign one group per role
Muting Set Switches off a permission in a group Other uses stay unchanged
Assignment Many sets per user One profile per user

Interview Q&A

1. Profile vs Permission Set?

A user has one profile as the baseline, and any number of permission sets that add extra access.

Tip: One profile, many sets.

2. Why prefer permission sets?

They follow least privilege: keep profiles minimal and grant extras only to the people who need them.

Tip: Fewer profiles, easier upkeep.

3. What is a Permission Set Group?

It bundles several permission sets into one unit you assign, usually matching a job role.

Tip: Assign one group per role.

4. What is a Muting Permission Set?

It lives inside a group and turns off chosen permissions from that group's sets, without editing the sets.

Tip: Mute, do not clone.

5. Can a permission set remove access?

A normal set only grants. To take access away, use a muting set or change the profile.

Tip: Access is additive.

6. What stays on the profile?

Login hours, login IP ranges, default record types and page layout assignments still live on the profile.

Tip: Name login hours and IP ranges.

Scenario Question

"Only 10 of 100 reps may export reports. How do you do it?"

  1. Keep one shared profile for all reps

  2. Create a permission set with Export Reports

  3. Assign it to the 10 users

  4. Bundle into a group if roles grow

Quick Cheat Sheet

  • Profile = baseline, one per user

  • Set = extra access, many per user

  • Group = bundle for a role

  • Muting = off inside a group

  • Additive = sets only grant

  • Profile-only = login hours, IPs

Key Takeaways

  • Keep profiles minimal

  • Grant extra access with sets

  • Group sets by job role

  • Document what each set is for

Which access would you move to a set first? Tell me in the comments!

Following my 30-day daily blogging journey. Day 14 done, 16 to go.

item.title: Salesforce Record Types & Page Layouts Cheat Sheet: Picklists, Assignment and Admin Interview Q&A (Day 13/30)
item.description: One object, many teams. Record types and page layouts show each team the fields, values and process it needs, and they come up in almost every admin…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
One object, many teams. Record types and page layouts show each team the fields, values and process it needs, and they come up in almost every admin interview.

The 4 Building Blocks

Block What it is Key point
Record Type Splits one object into variants Own picklists and process
Page Layout Fields, buttons, related lists Assigned by profile
Picklist Values Limited per record type Hide the ones not needed
Assignment Profile plus record type Picks the layout shown

Interview Q&A

1. What is a Record Type?

It lets one object serve different teams, each with its own picklist values, page layouts and business process.

Tip: Use it when processes differ.

2. What is a Page Layout?

It controls which fields, buttons, sections and related lists a user sees on a record.

Tip: Layouts shape the screen, not security.

3. How is a layout assigned?

By profile and record type together. Each pair gets one page layout.

Tip: Check the assignment matrix.

4. How do users get a record type?

Through their profile or a permission set. Without access, they cannot pick it.

Tip: Permission sets add types without editing the profile.

5. Layout vs field-level security?

A layout only hides a field on the page. Field-level security blocks access everywhere, including reports and the API.

Tip: Use FLS to truly protect data.

6. Page Layout vs Lightning Page?

Page layouts set fields and related lists. Lightning record pages set the overall page, components and dynamic forms.

Tip: Name both, then say which you use.

Scenario Question

"Support handles Billing and Technical cases with different fields. How do you do it?"

  1. Create two Case record types

  2. Limit the Status values for each type

  3. Build one page layout for each type

  4. Assign by profile and record type

Quick Cheat Sheet

  • Record type = variant of an object

  • Layout = fields and related lists

  • Picklist = values per type

  • Access = profile or permission set

  • FLS = real field security

  • Lightning page = overall page

Key Takeaways

  • Add types only when processes differ

  • Keep layouts simple and few

  • Never rely on layouts for security

  • Test as a real user

Which object would you split first? Tell me in the comments!

item.title: Salesforce Approval Processes Cheat Sheet: Entry Criteria, Approvers and Admin Interview Q&A (Day 12/30)
item.description: Some changes need a second pair of eyes. Approval processes route a record to the right person before it moves on, and they come up in almost every admin…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
Some changes need a second pair of eyes. Approval processes route a record to the right person before it moves on, and they come up in almost every admin interview that touches automation.

The 4 Building Blocks

Block What it is Key point
Entry Criteria Decides which records can be submitted Records that miss them cannot be submitted
Approval Step Who reviews the record User, queue, manager or field
Actions Run on submit, approve or reject Field update, email, task
Record Lock Record is read-only while pending Admins can still edit

Interview Q&A

1. What is an Approval Process?

It automates how a record gets approved: submit, route to approvers, then approve or reject, with actions at each stage.

Tip: Think of it as a manager sign-off.

2. What are entry criteria?

Conditions a record must meet before it can be submitted, like Discount over 20 percent.

Tip: Records that miss them cannot be submitted.

3. Who can be an approver?

A user, a queue, the submitter's manager, or a user picked from a field on the record.

Tip: Queues let a team share the work.

4. What actions can run?

Field updates, email alerts, tasks and outbound messages, on submit, final approval, final rejection or recall.

Tip: Use a field update to set Status.

5. What does the record lock do?

A pending record is locked so users cannot edit it. Admins can still edit, and a recall unlocks it.

Tip: The lock stops edits while review is open.

6. Approval Process vs Flow?

Approval Processes handle classic sign-off. Flow Orchestrator is the newer option for complex, multi-step approvals.

Tip: Name the trade-off, then pick.

Scenario Question

"Discounts over 20 percent need manager approval before the deal moves on. How do you do it?"

  1. Entry criteria: Discount greater than 20 percent

  2. Approver: the submitter's manager

  3. On submit: a field update sets Status to Pending

  4. On approval: Status becomes Approved

Quick Cheat Sheet

  • Entry = who may submit

  • Approver = user, queue, manager

  • Actions = update, email, task

  • Lock = read-only while pending

  • Recall = pulls it back

  • Orchestrator = newer option

Key Takeaways

  • Define entry criteria first

  • Prefer queues or managers over named users

  • Track status with field updates

  • Test with a real submitter

What would you send for approval first? Tell me in the comments!

item.title: Salesforce Validation Rules Cheat Sheet: Formulas, Error Messages and Admin Interview Q&A (Day 11/30)
item.description: Clean data starts at the door. Validation rules decide what Salesforce lets in, and what it turns away. They are one of the most asked-about admin topics…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
Clean data starts at the door. Validation rules decide what Salesforce lets in, and what it turns away. They are one of the most asked-about admin topics because every real org depends on them.

The 4 Data Quality Tools

Tool What it is Key point
Validation Rule Blocks a save if the formula is TRUE Shows your error message
Formula Field A read-only calculated value Recalculates automatically
Required Field Must have a value to save Set on the field or the layout
Duplicate Rule Warns or blocks likely duplicates Works with Matching Rules

Interview Q&A

1. What is a Validation Rule?

A formula that returns TRUE when data is bad. If it is TRUE, Salesforce blocks the save and shows your error message.

Tip: TRUE means error, FALSE means save.

2. Where does the error show?

You choose: at the top of the page, or next to a specific field on the record page.

Tip: Show it by the field the user must fix.

3. Required field vs Validation Rule?

A field-level required setting always applies, even through the API. A validation rule can add conditions, like required only at a certain stage.

Tip: Needed only sometimes? Use a rule.

4. Formula field vs Validation Rule?

A formula field returns a value users cannot edit. A validation rule formula returns TRUE or FALSE to allow or block a save.

Tip: Formula fields are read-only.

5. Which functions come up most?

ISBLANK for empty checks, ISPICKVAL for picklists, AND and OR to combine tests, ISCHANGED on updates, and REGEX for patterns.

Tip: Never compare a picklist with =.

6. Do rules run on imports and Flows?

Yes. They also run for the API, Apex and Flow. To skip them for admins or data loads, check a custom permission in the formula.

Tip: Avoid hardcoding profile names.

Scenario Question

"Reps must not mark an Opportunity Closed Won without an Amount. How do you enforce it?"

  1. Go to Object Manager, Opportunity, Validation Rules

  2. Write the formula with ISPICKVAL and ISBLANK

  3. Add a clear error message on the Amount field

  4. Test in a sandbox, then activate

The formula looks like this:

AND(
  ISPICKVAL(StageName, "Closed Won"),
  ISBLANK(Amount)
)

Quick Cheat Sheet

  • TRUE = block the save

  • ISBLANK = empty check

  • ISPICKVAL = picklist check

  • ISCHANGED = on updates

  • Formula field = read-only

  • Bypass = custom permission

Key Takeaways

  • Write the rule so TRUE means bad data

  • Keep error messages specific

  • Required field for always, rule for sometimes

  • Add a bypass for data loads

What is the best validation rule you have written? Tell me in the comments!

item.title: Salesforce Reports & Dashboards Cheat Sheet: Formats, Running User and Admin Interview Q&A (Day 10/30)
item.description: Reports answer the question, dashboards show the answer. Interviewers love this topic because it tests whether you can turn raw data into something a…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
Reports answer the question, dashboards show the answer. Interviewers love this topic because it tests whether you can turn raw data into something a manager can act on.

The 4 Report Formats

Format What it is Key point
Tabular A simple list of records No grouping, no dashboard charts
Summary Rows grouped by a field Up to 3 groupings, subtotals
Matrix Grouped by rows and columns Up to 2 row and 2 column groups
Joined Blocks from different report types Up to 5 blocks in one report

Interview Q&A

1. What is a Report Type?

It decides which objects and fields a report can use. Standard report types exist, and you can build custom report types with related objects.

Tip: "With" shows parents that have children, "with or without" shows all parents.

2. Summary vs Matrix report?

A Summary report groups rows by up to 3 fields. A Matrix report groups by both rows and columns, so you can compare two dimensions at once.

Tip: Need a cross-tab like region by quarter? Use a matrix.

3. Report vs Dashboard?

A report lists filtered records. A dashboard shows up to 20 components, each built from a source report.

Tip: Every component needs a source report.

4. Running user vs dynamic dashboard?

A normal dashboard shows data as seen by its running user. A dynamic dashboard runs as whoever is viewing it.

Tip: Use dynamic when each viewer should see only their own data.

5. What is a Bucket field?

It groups report values into categories you define, with no formula or custom field needed.

Tip: For example, group deal amounts into Small, Medium and Large.

6. What is a Cross filter?

It filters records by related records, like Accounts with or without Opportunities.

Tip: Great for finding accounts with no activity.

Scenario Question

"A sales manager wants open pipeline by stage as a dashboard, emailed weekly. How do you do it?"

  1. Build a Summary report on Opportunities, open only

  2. Group the report by Stage and add a chart

  3. Add it to a dashboard as a component

  4. Subscribe the manager for a weekly email

Quick Cheat Sheet

  • Tabular = simple list

  • Summary = up to 3 groupings

  • Matrix = rows and columns

  • Joined = up to 5 blocks

  • Dashboard = up to 20 components

  • Bucket = group without a formula

Key Takeaways

  • Choose the report type first

  • Summary to group, matrix to compare

  • Dashboards display reports

  • Check the running user

Summary or Matrix: which do you build most? Tell me in the comments!

item.title: Lookup vs Master-Detail: Salesforce Relationships Cheat Sheet for Admin Interviews (Day 9/30)
item.description: Relationships are the backbone of every Salesforce data model, and interviewers love them. Almost every question comes down to one idea: can the child…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
Relationships are the backbone of every Salesforce data model, and interviewers love them. Almost every question comes down to one idea: can the child record exist without its parent?

The 4 Relationship Types

Type What it is Key point
Lookup A loose link between two objects Optional, the child keeps its own owner
Master-Detail A tight parent-child bond Cascade delete, roll-ups, shared access
Junction object Links two objects many-to-many Two master-detail fields
Hierarchical Records link to the same object Parent Account, user manager

Interview Q&A

1. Standard vs Custom objects?

Standard objects ship with Salesforce, such as Account, Contact and Opportunity. Custom objects are built by you, and their API names end in __c.

Tip: Custom objects and fields always end in __c.

2. Lookup vs Master-Detail?

A Lookup is optional and loosely coupled. A Master-Detail is required: the child inherits the parent's owner and sharing.

Tip: Ask: can the child exist without the parent?

3. What is a Junction object?

A custom object with two master-detail fields that creates a many-to-many link, like Student to Course through Enrollment.

Tip: The first master-detail sets the owner and sharing.

4. What is a Roll-up Summary field?

It lives on the master record and calculates COUNT, SUM, MIN or MAX over its detail records. It is only available with master-detail.

Tip: Need it on a lookup? Use a Flow instead.

5. Can you convert between them?

Lookup to Master-Detail works only if every child record already has a parent. Master-Detail to Lookup works only if the parent has no roll-up summary fields.

Tip: Fill in blank lookups before converting.

6. What happens if the parent is deleted?

With Master-Detail the children are deleted too (cascade). With a Lookup the children stay, unless you restrict the delete.

Tip: Restricting delete protects child data.

Scenario Question

"A school tracks Students and Courses, and each student can take many courses. How do you model it?"

  1. Create custom objects Student and Course

  2. Create a junction object called Enrollment

  3. Add two master-detail fields: one to Student, one to Course

  4. Add a roll-up summary on Course to count Enrollments

Quick Cheat Sheet

  • Lookup = optional, independent

  • Master-Detail = required, cascade delete

  • Junction = two master-details

  • Roll-up = master-detail only

  • Max 2 master-detail fields per object

  • Custom API names end in __c

Key Takeaways

  • Start with: can the child exist alone?

  • Use master-detail for tight ownership

  • Use a junction object for many-to-many

  • Plan relationships before you build

Lookup or Master-Detail: which do you pick first? Tell me in the comments!

item.title: Salesforce Flow Cheat Sheet: Types, Triggers and Admin Interview Q&A (Day 8/30)
item.description: Flow is now the one automation tool every Salesforce Admin is expected to know. Interviewers usually ask the same few things: which type, which trigger…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
Flow is now the one automation tool every Salesforce Admin is expected to know. Interviewers usually ask the same few things: which type, which trigger timing, and how you keep it safe at scale.

The 4 Flow Types

Type Use it when Examples
Screen Flow A user needs to click and type Guided forms, wizards, Lightning pages
Record-Triggered Flow A record is created, updated or deleted Update a field, create a task
Scheduled-Triggered Flow Something must run at a set time Daily or weekly batch jobs
Autolaunched Flow Another process calls it Called from flows, Apex, buttons

Interview Q&A

1. What is a Record-Triggered Flow?

It runs automatically when a record is created, updated or deleted. Entry conditions decide when it actually fires.

Tip: Add entry conditions so it only runs when needed.

2. Before-save vs After-save?

Before-save updates the same record that triggered the flow, fast, with no extra DML. After-save handles related records, emails and other actions.

Tip: Same record = before. Anything else = after.

3. Flow vs Workflow Rules and Process Builder?

Workflow Rules and Process Builder are retired, with support ending on Dec 31, 2025. Flow is the single automation tool going forward.

Tip: Say you would migrate old automation to Flow.

4. Flow or Apex?

Start with clicks, not code. Use Apex when logic is very complex, needs heavy bulk processing, or Flow cannot do it.

Tip: "Declarative first" is the safe answer.

5. What are the data elements?

Get, Create, Update and Delete Records. Get Records reads data into variables you can reuse.

Tip: One well-filtered Get Records beats many.

6. Why never put DML in a loop?

Governor limits cap queries and DML per transaction. Collect records in a collection variable, then do one DML after the loop.

Tip: Add a Fault path and test with Debug.

Scenario Question

"When an Opportunity becomes Closed Won, create a follow-up Task and update the Account. How?"

  1. Build a Record-Triggered Flow on Opportunity, run after save

  2. Entry condition: Stage = Closed Won and Stage is changed

  3. Create Records: a Task for the Account owner

  4. Update Records: the Account, add a Fault path, then test with Debug

Quick Cheat Sheet

  • Screen = user input

  • Record-Triggered = on create, update, delete

  • Scheduled = runs at a set time

  • Autolaunched = called by others

  • Before-save = fast, same record

  • No DML in loops

Key Takeaways

  • Flow first, Apex only when needed

  • Choose before-save or after-save on purpose

  • Use entry conditions to limit runs

  • Always add Fault paths and test with Debug

Which Flow type do you use most? Tell me in the comments!

item.title: Salesforce Security Model Cheat Sheet: 4 Layers and Admin Interview Q&A (Day 7/30)
item.description: Security questions come up in almost every Salesforce Admin interview. The good news: the whole model fits in one picture. Think of it as four locks on…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
Security questions come up in almost every Salesforce Admin interview. The good news: the whole model fits in one picture. Think of it as four locks on four doors, and every question is really asking "which lock is this?"

This is the quick cheat sheet version. For the long, step-by-step walkthrough, read my earlier post: The Salesforce Security Model Explained: OWD, Roles, Sharing Rules and More.

The Big Picture: 4 Layers of Access

Layer Question it answers Tools
Org level Can this person log in at all? Password policies, login hours, login IP ranges, MFA
Object level Can they see or edit this type of data? Profiles, Permission Sets
Field level Can they see this column? Field-Level Security (FLS)
Record level Can they see this row? OWD, Role Hierarchy, Sharing Rules, Manual Sharing

Golden rule: Object and field access decide what kind of data you can touch. Record access decides which rows you can touch. You need both.

Interview Q&A

1. What is a Profile?

A profile controls what a user can do: which objects and fields they can access, which apps and tabs they see, and system permissions. Every user has exactly one profile.

Tip: Say "profile = baseline permissions". It sets up your next answer about permission sets.

2. What is a Permission Set, and how is it different from a Profile?

A permission set adds access on top of a profile. A user can have many permission sets, but only one profile. Permission sets can only grant access, never take it away.

Tip: Mention best practice: keep profiles minimal and grant extra access through permission sets (and Permission Set Groups to bundle them).

3. What is OWD (Organization-Wide Defaults)?

OWD sets the baseline record access for each object. It is the most restrictive level in the system, and every other tool (roles, sharing rules) can only open access up from there.

Common settings: Private, Public Read Only, Public Read/Write, Controlled by Parent.

Tip: Always say "start restrictive, then open up".

4. What is the Role Hierarchy?

Roles control record visibility upward. A manager can see the records owned by people below them in the hierarchy. Roles do not give object permissions; that is the profile's job.

Tip: The classic trap question: "Profile vs Role?" Profile = what you can do. Role = which records you can see.

5. What are Sharing Rules?

Sharing rules open access to records for groups of users when OWD is restrictive. They can be based on record owner or on record criteria (for example, Region = West).

Tip: Remember sharing rules only extend access. They can never restrict it.

6. What is Field-Level Security?

FLS controls whether a user can see or edit a specific field, set through profiles or permission sets. Hidden fields disappear from page layouts, reports and list views.

Tip: A page layout alone does not secure a field. FLS does.

7. What is Manual Sharing?

The record owner (or a user with full access) can share an individual record with a specific user or group. It is useful for one-off exceptions.

Tip: Manual sharing is lost if the record owner changes, so don't build a process around it.

8. If two settings conflict, which one wins?

Access in Salesforce is additive: the most permissive result wins. Two permission sources never cancel each other out.

Scenario Question (Very Common!)

"Sales reps should only see their own accounts. Managers should see their team's accounts. How do you set that up?"

  1. Set Account OWD = Private

  2. Build the Role Hierarchy with managers above reps

  3. Keep Grant Access Using Hierarchies enabled

  4. If one team needs to see another team's accounts, add a Sharing Rule

Result: reps see their own records, managers see their whole team's, no extra code needed.

Quick Cheat Sheet

  • Profile = baseline permissions (one per user)

  • Permission Set = extra permissions (many per user)

  • OWD = the most restrictive baseline for records

  • Role Hierarchy = upward record visibility

  • Sharing Rules = open access to groups

  • FLS = field-level visibility

  • Most permissive wins

Key Takeaways

  • Answer in layers: org, object, field, record

  • Use a real example for every answer

  • Always separate "what you can do" (profile) from "what you can see" (role)

  • Keep it simple, and explain why each tool exists

Which part of the Salesforce security model confused you the most when you were learning it? Tell me in the comments!

item.title: AWS VPC for Beginners: Subnets, Route Tables, Gateways and Security Groups
item.description: Beginner's guide to AWS VPC: CIDR blocks, public and private subnets, internet and NAT gateways, route tables, security groups and NACLs.
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
A Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) is your own private network inside AWS. Every EC2 instance, RDS database and many Lambda functions live in one. Networking was the part of AWS that confused me most at first, so here is the explanation I wish I'd had.

The VPC and its CIDR block

When you create a VPC, you give it an IP range in CIDR notation, for example:

10.0.0.0/16   →   65,536 addresses (10.0.0.0 – 10.0.255.255)

A VPC lives in one region but spans all of that region's Availability Zones.

Subnets

A subnet is a slice of the VPC's range in one Availability Zone:

10.0.1.0/24   public subnet   (AZ a)
10.0.2.0/24   public subnet   (AZ b)
10.0.11.0/24  private subnet  (AZ a)
10.0.12.0/24  private subnet  (AZ b)

AWS reserves 5 addresses in every subnet, so a /24 gives you 251 usable IPs.

Public vs private isn't a setting. It depends on the subnet's route table.

Internet Gateway

An Internet Gateway (IGW) connects the VPC to the internet. A subnet is public when its route table sends internet traffic to the IGW:

Destination     Target
10.0.0.0/16     local
0.0.0.0/0       igw-xxxx

Instances in it also need a public IP to be reachable.

NAT Gateway

Instances in private subnets often still need to reach the internet (to download updates, for example) without being reachable from it. A NAT Gateway sits in a public subnet and handles that:

Private subnet route table
Destination     Target
10.0.0.0/16     local
0.0.0.0/0       nat-xxxx

NAT Gateways are charged per hour plus per GB processed, so they're often one of the bigger networking costs. For high availability, use one per AZ.

Route tables

Every subnet is associated with one route table. The local route (VPC CIDR → local) is always there, so everything inside the VPC can talk to everything else unless security rules block it.

Security groups vs network ACLs

Security Group Network ACL
Applies to Network interfaces (instances) Subnets
Rules Allow only Allow and deny
State Stateful (return traffic allowed automatically) Stateless (must allow return traffic explicitly)
Evaluation All rules together In number order, first match wins

In practice, security groups do most of the work. A common pattern is referencing one security group from another, for example: "the database security group allows port 5432 only from the app security group."

A classic three-tier layout

Internet
   │
Internet Gateway
   │
Public subnets   →  Load balancer, NAT Gateway
   │
Private subnets  →  App servers (EC2 / ECS)
   │
Private subnets  →  Database (RDS)

Only the load balancer is exposed. App servers and databases stay private.

Other pieces you'll meet

  • VPC endpoints – reach services like S3 or DynamoDB privately, without a NAT Gateway (and often more cheaply)
  • VPC peering / Transit Gateway – connect VPCs together
  • VPC Flow Logs – record traffic metadata for troubleshooting and security

Troubleshooting connectivity

When something can't connect, check in this order:

  1. Route table of the source subnet
  2. Security group on the destination (inbound) and source (outbound)
  3. Network ACLs on both subnets (remember return traffic)
  4. Public IP / Elastic IP if internet access is involved
  5. VPC Flow Logs to see whether traffic was accepted or rejected

Once you can draw your VPC on paper, most networking problems become much easier to solve.
